question: If \(t=\dfrac1{1-\sqrt[4]{2}},\) then \(t\) equals
solution:
Let \(r=\sqrt[4]{2}=\sqrt{\sqrt2}\), so \(r^2=\sqrt2\) and \(r^4=2\). Multiplying by \(1+r\) replaces \(r\) in the denominator by \(r^2\). A second difference of squares then removes the remaining radical.

Since \(r>1\), the denominators below are nonzero. We obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
t&=\frac1{1-r}\\
&=\frac{1+r}{1-r^2}\\
&=\frac{(1+r)(1+r^2)}{1-r^4}\\
&=-(1+r)(1+\sqrt2).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(t=-(1+\sqrt[4]{2})(1+\sqrt2)\), choice E.
